opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think code review is one of those places where the bottleneck has really shifted. As models got better at writing code, teams started producing a lot more of it, and suddenly the constraint isn't how fast you can write a change, it's how confidently you can merge it. Human reviewers only have so much attention, and reviewing is honestly a pretty draining task when you're doing it all day.

What we've found with Codex code review is that it's really good at the part that's hard for people to sustain: actually going deep on every single PR. It doesn't just skim the diff. It can navigate the codebase, understand the context around the change, look at how a function is used elsewhere, and in some cases run code to check its hypotheses. So it catches things like subtle logic bugs, edge cases, or a change that quietly breaks an assumption somewhere else in the system, the kinds of issues that slip through when a reviewer is on their tenth PR of the afternoon.

We've also been careful about signal-to-noise. A reviewer that leaves fifty nitpicky comments is worse than useless, because people learn to ignore it. So we've focused on making it flag fewer, higher-value issues, things where if it speaks up, you should probably pay attention. Internally at OpenAI, that's been the key to adoption. Engineers actually look forward to the review, and there have been plenty of cases where it caught a bug that would have caused a real incident.

The way I think about it is that it doesn't replace human review, it raises the floor. Humans can focus on design, architecture, whether this is the right thing to build at all, while Codex makes sure the details are correct. And as we generate more and more code with agents, having that safety net becomes essential. It lets teams move faster without trading away quality or trust in what they're shipping.

r001.rationale: It says teams produce more code while human reviewers have limited attention, making confident merging the constraint.

r002.rationale: It mentions finding logic bugs, edge cases, and broken assumptions, but does not clearly describe checking an implementation against its intended behavioral contract.

r003.rationale: It describes deep review and catching subtle issues, but does not say these are issues that even expert human reviewers would need hours of investigation to find.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The reason I find code review so exciting is that it's actually the part of the engineering workflow where you get a very clear win, and the win compounds across the whole team.

If you think about what happens when you write code with an agent, you get a lot of leverage on the production side. You can generate pull requests much faster than before. But that just moves the bottleneck. Now someone has to read all of it, and reading code carefully is hard, it's tiring, and it's where a lot of mistakes slip through because reviewers are busy and context-switching all day.

What Codex does in review is different from what a traditional linter or a static analysis tool does. It actually reads the pull request in the context of the whole repository. It tries to understand the intent of the change, what the author was trying to accomplish, and then it asks: does the code actually do that? Are there edge cases that were missed? Does this break something three directories away that the author never looked at? It can navigate the codebase, trace call sites, and sometimes even run things to validate a hypothesis before it leaves a comment.

And the thing we've optimized for pretty deliberately is signal over noise. A review tool that leaves thirty stylistic nitpicks on every PR gets ignored within a week. So the goal is for Codex to only flag things that are genuinely worth a human's attention, real bugs, security issues, logic errors, and to explain them with enough evidence that the engineer can trust the finding without re-deriving it themselves.

Internally at OpenAI, the vast majority of our PRs now go through Codex review, and the feedback from engineers is that it catches things they would have shipped. That's the real value. It's not about replacing the human reviewer, it's about making sure that by the time a human looks at the change, the obvious and the subtle-but-mechanical problems are already surfaced, so they can spend their attention on design and whether this is the right thing to build at all.

For teams, that translates into fewer incidents, faster merges, and honestly a bit less dread around the review queue. That's a pretty good outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says faster PR generation moves the bottleneck to someone reading the increased volume of code, which is difficult and tiring for busy reviewers.

r002.rationale: It says Codex considers the author’s intent and checks whether the code actually accomplishes it, including missed edge cases and downstream breakage.

r003.rationale: The response says Codex catches issues engineers might have shipped, but does not state that it finds issues requiring expert human reviewers to spend hours investigating.

astra-6.text:
I think code review is valuable because writing code is only part of the work. You also have to understand whether a change does what you intended, whether it introduces a bug, and how it interacts with the rest of the system. That takes a lot of attention from engineers.

Codex can give you another pass over a change and flag potential issues before a teammate gets involved. That can shorten the feedback loop for the author and let human reviewers spend more time on questions like whether the design makes sense or whether you’re solving the right problem.

The key is making that feedback useful. You want it to point out meaningful issues and explain why they matter. If it can consistently do that, it helps teams move faster while maintaining confidence in the code they ship.

r001.rationale: It says code review takes engineers' attention, but does not connect human review capacity becoming a bottleneck to increasing review volume.

r002.rationale: It says Codex can check whether a change does what the author intended, which communicates checking the implementation against its intended behavior.

r003.rationale: It says Codex can flag potential issues, but does not state that it can find issues requiring expert reviewers hours of deep investigation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think code review is valuable because writing code is only part of the work. You also need confidence that the change does what you intended and doesn’t break something else. Codex can provide another set of eyes, catch potential issues, and give engineers feedback before they ask a teammate to review.

That lets the team spend more of its attention on the questions that need human judgment: Is this the right design? Does it solve the user’s problem? The value is helping engineers catch mistakes earlier and making the review conversation more productive.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex can give engineers feedback before teammate review, but does not identify human review capacity as a bottleneck or connect it to increasing code volume.

r002.rationale: It says Codex can help check that a change “does what you intended,” which communicates checking whether the implementation fulfills its intended behavior.

r003.rationale: It mentions catching potential issues, but does not say Codex can uncover issues that expert human reviewers would need hours of deep investigation to find.
